text: What legal AI use cases are safe to start with, and where should Legal avoid automation?
claudePromptBoundary: Full production prompt is reconstructed from current source template and captured source packet. ai_egress_audit stores prompt hash/snapshot refs, not raw prompt text by default.
claudeResponse:
Lakeshore Holdings is in a realistic position on Legal AI — the loaded evidence is enough to start carefully, but not enough to scale confidently. The honest
Legal should begin with two low-risk, high-visibility use cases while holding off on anything that touches privileged content, litigation strategy, or binding legal judgment. Where Legal can safely start: The contract renewal risk summarizer is already in your AI initiative inventory.
This is the right first move — Ironclad CLM is live, contract obligations and renewals are a named data asset, and the weighted average review cycle time baseline is loaded at 16 days with a Finance-approved improvement target of 8–12% in pilot. That's a measurable, bounded use case with a real KPI. Start there.
The second safe bet is matter and document triage — using AI to classify incoming requests, route to the right attorney or outside counsel queue, and flag renewal deadlines. Low privilege risk, high friction reduction, and it builds the data foundation Legal will need for anything more ambitious later.
Where Legal should not automate yet: Avoid automating anything that produces legal advice, interprets regulatory obligations, or generates language that goes into executed contracts without attorney review.
The loaded sources flag that outside counsel avoidance savings are "directional" and require evidence before board use — that's a signal the economics aren't proven and the control model isn't defined.
Privilege boundaries, privacy constraints, and matter confidentiality are also explicit evidence gaps in the current packet; until those are mapped, any AI touching matter data or correspondence is a liability, not an asset. The practical sequencing: treat Legal as a Phase 2 discovery branch alongside HR.
The CIO should commission a Legal process-volume and data-readiness exercise — CLM process volumes, eBilling and matter data access, policy and contract request taxonomy, and privilege boundary mapping — before recommending anything beyond the contract summarizer pilot. That discovery work is what unlocks a credible Legal AI roadmap.
The next useful decision is whether the General Counsel is ready to co-own the CLM pilot KPI with Legal Ops and IT, or whether Legal AI stays a CIO-driven initiative without a business-side owner. Without that co-ownership, the 8–12% cycle-time target stays aspirational. --- Legal AI — Safe Start vs.
Hold | Use Case | Safety Posture | System / Data | KPI Anchor | Risk / Constraint | Posture |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Contract renewal risk summarizer | Safe to pilot | Ironclad CLM; contract obligations data asset | Review cycle time: 16 days → 8–12% improvement target | Scope to renewal flags only; no contract drafting | Start now |
| Matter and request triage / routing | Safe to pilot | Ironclad CLM; M365 | Intake volume deflection; routing accuracy | Keep human-in-the-loop for all privilege-touching matters | Start now |
| Outside counsel spend analytics | Conditional | CLM / eBilling (not confirmed loaded) | Outside counsel avoidance — directional only per CFO note | eBilling data access and matter confidentiality must be confirmed first | Shape next |
| Contract language generation / drafting | Hold | CLM + attorney review workflow | N/A until attorney-in-the-loop model is defined | Executed contract liability; brand and legal risk | Hold |
| Regulatory interpretation / legal advice | Avoid | N/A | N/A | Privilege, liability, and regulatory risk — not automatable | Do not automate |
| Litigation strategy or matter assessment | Avoid | N/A | N/A | Requires attorney judgment; AI output not defensible in court | Do not automate |
